title: "Stash"

# Stash Mechanics, Including Patch Stashes

After this page you can park uncommitted work, switch branches, and bring the work back.

## A stash is a commit Git keeps on the side

```bash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "wip" >> README.md
git stash push -m "wip readme"
git status
git stash list
```

Working tree is clean. `stash@{0}` holds the diff. Switch branches, then:

```text
 before stash                 after stash push

 working  dirty README        working  clean
 index    clean               index    clean
 HEAD     C                   HEAD     C
                              stash@{0}  ──► a pair of commits
                                           (index + working tree)
```

```bash
git stash pop
# or
git stash apply
```

`pop` applies and drops. `apply` applies and keeps the stash entry.

## Include untracked

```bash
git stash push -u -m "wip plus new files"
```

Without `-u`, untracked files stay in the way and can block a switch.

## Patch stash (`-p`)

```bash
git stash push -p -m "only the ping hunk"
```

Git offers hunks, same as `git add -p`. Stash the ones that are in the way; leave the rest in the working tree.

## Named and multiple

```bash
git stash push -m "experiment A"
git stash push -m "experiment B"
git stash list
git stash apply stash@{1}
git stash drop stash@{1}
git stash show -p stash@{0}
```

Numbers shift when you drop. The message is how you find them.

## Conflicts on apply

Markers appear. Add and continue as a normal working-tree conflict. The stash entry remains if you used `apply`; `pop` may still drop — prefer `apply` when you are unsure.

## Stash vs commit

A commit on a throwaway branch is easier to push and to recover. Stash is for “I must switch in the next ten seconds.” If the WIP will last, `git switch -c wip/…` and commit.
